mcqs.question: Why can't you determine which portion of an IP address is the network and which is the host from the address alone?
options: Because the same 32-bit address can be split at different bit boundaries depending on the prefix length (mask), so the split requires that extra piece of information
Because IP addresses are randomly assigned with no structure at all
Because only IPv6 addresses have a network/host split; IPv4 addresses don't
Because the network portion is always exactly the first octet, regardless of context
mcqs.explanation: The address's bits are fixed, but where the network/host boundary falls within those bits depends entirely on the prefix length — the same address means different things under /24 vs /26. IP addresses aren't random (the claim that addresses are randomly assigned is false), IPv4 absolutely has this split (the claim that IPv4 lacks a network/host split is false), and the boundary is not fixed at the first octet — that's only true for old classful Class C (the claim that the network portion is always the first octet is false in general).

mcqs.question: A 1990s company needing addresses for 300 hosts was forced to take a full Class B allocation (65,536 addresses) under classful addressing. Why was this wasteful, and what replaced it?
options: It wasn't actually wasteful — classful addressing was always efficient

Classful addressing only offered fixed-size blocks (A/B/C), so a need slightly above a Class C's 254 hosts forced allocating an entire Class B; CIDR replaced it by allowing any prefix length to fit the exact need
The waste was fixed by adding a Class D specifically for mid-size networks
IPv6 was introduced specifically to fix this exact allocation problem in the 1990s
mcqs.explanation: The core problem was classful addressing's fixed granularity — no size existed between a 254-host Class C and a 65K-host Class B, forcing gross over-allocation. CIDR's variable prefix lengths fixed exactly this. Class D is reserved for multicast, not general host allocation (the claim that a new Class D fixed it is false), and IPv6 addresses a different problem (total exhaustion), arriving later and not as the direct 1990s fix (the claim that IPv6 was the direct 1990s fix is false).

mcqs.question: A laptop shows an IP address of 169.254.34.12 and can't reach anything outside its own subnet. What does this address specifically indicate?
options: The laptop successfully received a valid address from the DHCP server
The laptop is using a private RFC 1918 address correctly configured for its LAN
This is a link-local (APIPA) self-assigned address, meaning DHCP failed and the OS fell back to self-assignment — it's a specific, diagnosable signal, not general network breakage
This is the loopback address indicating the laptop is only able to talk to itself
mcqs.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is the reserved link-local/APIPA range specifically used when DHCP fails — it's a precise, actionable diagnostic signal. It is the opposite of a successful DHCP lease (the claim that DHCP succeeded is false), it isn't an RFC 1918 private range (the claim that it's an RFC 1918 private address is false), and loopback is the separate 127.0.0.0/8 range (the claim that it's the loopback address is false).
